title: Understanding Reactivity and Aggression, Part 1
notes: v6: Chapter 1 from the trainer's edited Google Doc (pages 1 to 7, everything above 'END OF FIRST CHAPTER MATERIAL'). Twelve scenes. Material below that line is not part of this video. v5 is in script/archive/lesson-v5-chapter1-10scenes.json. The trainer records the narration herself.

chapters.title: Aggression and Reactivity: Starting with the Basics

scenes.heading: Aggression and reactivity
scenes.visual_concept: Two photo circles (aggression, reactivity) under the heading. Aggression chips plus 'Behavior with intent.', the smoke alarm and toast under reactivity, then the circles slide into a Venn with a light green overlap. Ends with a 'Label' tag on the overlap and an arrow to a green 'Starting point' card.

beats.say: Let's start with two words you'll hear a lot: aggression and reactivity. They're not the same thing, and they can overlap.
beats.show: The heading 'Aggression and reactivity' writes on in green; the snarling dog photo and the barking white dog photo slide in as two large circles side by side, labeled 'Aggression' and 'Reactivity'.

beats.say: Aggression is behavior intended to threaten, push away, control, protect, or cause harm. It can show up in very different situations.
beats.show: Under the aggression circle, five small chips pop in one per word: Threaten, Push away, Control, Protect, Harm. A sixth line appears: 'Behavior with intent.'

beats.say: Reactivity is an intense, over-the-top response to something in the environment. Think of a smoke alarm that screams every time you make toast.
beats.show: Under the reactivity circle, a smoke alarm icon appears beside a tiny toast icon; red sound rings swell huge while the toast stays small.

beats.say: A reactive response can include aggressive behavior, but it doesn't have to. And aggressive behavior alone doesn't tell us what the dog is feeling or exactly what the behavior is accomplishing.
beats.show: The two circles slide together into a Venn diagram and the overlap tints light green.
beats.onscreen: They can overlap, but they're not the same

beats.say: That's why the label is only the starting point.
beats.show: A 'Label' tag lands on the overlap and a green arrow runs from it to a card: 'The starting point, not the whole story'.
beats.onscreen: The label is only the starting point

scenes.heading: Look beyond the label
scenes.visual_concept: A row of behavior chips, then one big BARK chip with four simple situations around it (each a small icon scene with its meaning), then those stay while 'Same behavior. Different context.' lands, then they fade and question marks gather around a dog icon.

beats.say: A dog may bark, growl, lunge, snap, freeze, cower, move away, or bite. These behaviors matter, but the behavior alone does not tell us why the dog is responding that way.
beats.show: The heading 'Look beyond the label' writes on in green and eight behavior chips pop in a row, one per word: Bark, Growl, Lunge, Snap, Freeze, Cower, Move away, Bite.

beats.say: Take barking. One dog may bark at a person because it wants the person to come closer. Another dog may bark because it wants the person to go away. Another may bark because it wants access to something the person has. And another may bark because the situation has become too overwhelming.
beats.show: A single large 'BARK' chip sits at center and four simple situations appear around it, one per sentence: Person at window, 'Come closer'; Person approaching, 'Go away'; Person holding toy, 'Give me that'; Overactive environment, 'Too much'.
beats.onscreen: The same behavior can have different reasons

beats.say: The behavior is the same, but why it's happening in each situation is different. And that difference matters when we decide how to help the dog.
beats.show: The four examples remain on screen while the central 'BARK' chip stays unchanged; the four situations glow in turn.

beats.say: So what influences how a dog responds in the first place? There are many factors that contribute to behavior. In this video, we'll take a closer look at some of the influences that shape how a dog responds.
beats.show: The four examples fade out and several question marks appear around a dog icon.

scenes.heading: Why?
scenes.visual_concept: Photo card and the heading 'Why?', then the bowl with eight blank ingredient chips hovering, then the chips start moving toward the bowl. Bowl chips, in order: Genetics and temperament, Prenatal environment, Breed history and purpose, Socialization, Age, Past experiences, Training tools and methods, Pain and discomfort (shared module video/scenes/c1_bowl.js).

beats.say: When a dog's behavior changes, one of the first questions an owner may ask is, "Why is my dog acting this way?"
beats.show: The Lab and Pyrenees photo slides in as a portrait card at left, and the heading 'Why?' writes on in green.

beats.say: The answer? It's not just one reason. A dog's behavior is influenced by many factors, which can contribute to fearful, reactive, aggressive, or other responses.
beats.show: The photo slides away; a large mixing bowl appears center right with eight blank ingredient chips hovering above it.

beats.say: Think of it like a recipe. There are several ingredients that can contribute to the behavior we see.
beats.show: The blank ingredient chips begin drifting down toward the bowl as the section transitions into the factors covered in this video.

scenes.heading: Genetics and temperament
scenes.visual_concept: Bowl scene. The Genetics and temperament chip drops in, then a tiny smoke alarm blinks for the sensitive dog. Bowl chips, in order: Genetics and temperament, Prenatal environment, Breed history and purpose, Socialization, Age, Past experiences, Training tools and methods, Pain and discomfort (shared module video/scenes/c1_bowl.js).

beats.say: Ingredient one: genetics. Dogs are born with different temperaments and personality traits. Some are naturally more sensitive to their surroundings, while others may be more easygoing or less reactive to change.
beats.show: The first chip, a DNA icon labeled 'Genetics and temperament', drops into the bowl with a small splash. Two small dog badges appear on the left, one labeled 'More sensitive' and one labeled 'More easygoing'.
beats.onscreen: Some dogs are born more sensitive

beats.say: Some dogs simply start life with a more sensitive "smoke alarm," meaning their nervous system may be more easily triggered from the beginning.
beats.show: A tiny smoke alarm icon blinks beside the 'More sensitive' dog with small red sound rings.

scenes.heading: Before birth
scenes.visual_concept: Bowl scene. The Prenatal environment chip drops in beside the DNA chip, with three icons around it. Bowl chips, in order: Genetics and temperament, Prenatal environment, Breed history and purpose, Socialization, Age, Past experiences, Training tools and methods, Pain and discomfort (shared module video/scenes/c1_bowl.js).

beats.say: Ingredient two: prenatal environment. A puppy's starting point can be influenced before it is even born. The mother's health, nutrition, and experiences during pregnancy can influence fetal development. These early influences can become part of the foundation a puppy starts life with.
beats.show: The DNA chip stays in the bowl as a second chip labeled 'Prenatal environment' drops in. Simple icons appear around it, one per word: a pregnant dog (health), a food bowl (nutrition), and a stress symbol (experiences).

scenes.heading: Breed history and purpose
scenes.visual_concept: Six AKC breed groups as six cards (three rows of two), each with a dog photo, the group name and a short job line; each card highlights and its photo appears as it is discussed. Ends with the cards flying into the bowl as the 'Breed history and purpose' chip. Bowl chips: Genetics and temperament, Prenatal environment, Breed history and purpose, Socialization, Age, Past experiences, Training tools and methods, Pain and discomfort (shared module video/scenes/c1_bowl.js).

beats.say: Ingredient three: breed history and purpose. Dogs have been selectively bred for generations to perform specific jobs. The American Kennel Club sorts many breeds into groups based on those jobs, and they can give us clues about behaviors a dog may be naturally inclined toward.
beats.show: Six AKC breed-group cards appear in a grid of three rows and two columns, each with an empty photo area, the group name and a short job line: Sporting Group: Find, flush, or retrieve game; Hound Group: Pursue game by sight or scent; Working Group: Guard, pull, rescue and other jobs; Terrier Group: Hunt vermin and small animals; Toy Group: Bred for companionship; Herding Group: Control and move livestock. A small label reads 'AKC breed groups'.
beats.onscreen: What was this dog bred to do?

beats.say: Those original jobs can influence the kinds of things a dog notices, how they respond to movement or their environment, and what behaviors they may be more likely to offer.
beats.show: All six cards pulse gently together.

beats.say: For example, sporting dogs were bred to assist hunters by finding, flushing, or retrieving game, like Golden Retrievers, Labrador Retrievers, Pointers, and Spaniels. Depending on the breed, that can mean being especially attentive to movement, searching, carrying objects, or working closely with a person.
beats.show: The Sporting Group card highlights while the others dim; its dog photo fades in with a small breed tag, and the example breeds appear under the card: Golden Retrievers, Labrador Retrievers, Pointers, Spaniels.

beats.say: Hounds were bred to pursue game, using either sight or scent, like Beagles, Bloodhounds, Greyhounds, and Dachshunds. A hound may be especially motivated to chase something fast or follow a scent that has captured their attention.
beats.show: The Hound Group card highlights while the others dim; its dog photo fades in with a small breed tag, and the example breeds appear under the card: Beagles, Bloodhounds, Greyhounds, Dachshunds.

beats.say: Working dogs were bred for jobs such as guarding property, pulling, rescue, and other working tasks, like Rottweilers, Great Danes, Siberian Huskies, and Newfoundlands. Those jobs can come with tendencies such as persistence, physical engagement, or close attention to unfamiliar people and activity around their home.
beats.show: The Working Group card highlights while the others dim; its dog photo fades in with a small breed tag, and the example breeds appear under the card: Rottweilers, Great Danes, Siberian Huskies, Newfoundlands.

beats.say: Terriers were bred primarily to hunt and eliminate vermin and other small animals, like Parson Russell Terriers, Airedale Terriers, and Miniature Schnauzers. Some may be particularly interested in quick movement from squirrels, cats, or other small animals.
beats.show: The Terrier Group card highlights while the others dim; its dog photo fades in with a small breed tag, and the example breeds appear under the card: Parson Russell Terriers, Airedale Terriers, Miniature Schnauzers.

beats.say: Toy breeds are small companion dogs, bred primarily for companionship, like Chihuahuas, Pomeranians, Maltese, and Yorkshire Terriers. Many are closely tuned in to their people, and because they're small, being picked up, loomed over, or crowded can feel like a much bigger deal.
beats.show: The Toy Group card highlights while the others dim; its dog photo fades in with a small breed tag, and the example breeds appear under the card: Chihuahuas, Pomeranians, Maltese, Yorkshire Terriers.

beats.say: And herding dogs were bred to control and move livestock, like German Shepherd Dogs, Border Collies, Australian Shepherds, and Corgis. Some may be especially tuned in to things that move and may naturally want to follow, control, or redirect that movement.
beats.show: The Herding Group card highlights while the others dim; its dog photo fades in with a small breed tag, and the example breeds appear under the card: German Shepherd Dogs, Border Collies, Australian Shepherds, Corgis. Then all six cards stay visible with their photos.

beats.say: That doesn't mean a dog will automatically behave a certain way because of its breed. Breed history gives us clues about tendencies, not guarantees.
beats.show: The line 'Breed history gives us clues, not guarantees.' lands over the cards.
beats.onscreen: Breed history gives us clues, not guarantees.

beats.say: Individual dogs can vary considerably, even within the same breed or mix. But when we're trying to understand a dog's behavior, knowing what those breeds were originally developed to do can give us another piece of the puzzle.
beats.show: The six cards move into the mixing bowl and become the 'Breed history and purpose' chip, which settles beside 'Genetics and temperament' and 'Prenatal environment'.

scenes.heading: Early life and socialization
scenes.visual_concept: Bowl scene. Socialization chip and the early-window timeline with gaps and example tags; a puppy observing a person, a dog and a new place from different distances with approach, move away and pause arrows; pass the puppy with a choice meter; the puppy surrounded by reaching hands with a pause icon and exit arrow just out of reach; the party row with a tightening leash; the chip settles. Bowl chips, in order: Genetics and temperament, Prenatal environment, Breed history and purpose, Socialization, Age, Past experiences, Training tools and methods, Pain and discomfort (shared module video/scenes/c1_bowl.js).

beats.say: Ingredient four, socialization. Early experiences help puppies learn what is familiar, safe, and normal. There is an important developmental period during the first few months when puppies are especially influenced by what they encounter.
beats.show: The 'Socialization' chip lights up above the bowl, and a timeline appears beside it with an early developmental window highlighted and labeled 'First few months'.

beats.say: When puppies don't have enough positive, appropriate exposure during this period, unfamiliar people, animals, places, or experiences may be harder for them to accept later. And if you adopt an older dog, some of what shaped their early expectations happened before you ever met them.
beats.show: Gaps appear in the highlighted window, and example tags appear along the timeline: Strangers, Buses, Skateboards, New places.

beats.say: But appropriate socialization isn't simply about exposing a puppy to as many things as possible. The way those experiences happen matters too. Puppies need opportunities to observe, approach, move away, and take a break. They should have some choice in whether and how they interact with something new.
beats.show: The timeline clears. A puppy watches a person, a dog and a new place from different distances; small arrows show its options, one per word: Observe, Approach, Move away, Take a break.

beats.say: Think about the game "pass the puppy." A well-meaning group of people may take turns picking up a puppy, holding them, petting them, and passing them from person to person. The puppy may have very little choice about what is happening or when they get a break.
beats.show: A puppy icon moves from one person icon to the next around a circle, with hands reaching toward it. A small 'Choice' meter stays near empty.

beats.say: Even when the people involved have good intentions, repeated handling without an opportunity to pause, move away, or choose whether to interact can make those experiences overwhelming rather than helpful.
beats.show: The puppy stays surrounded by reaching hands while a pause icon and an exit arrow sit just out of reach.

beats.say: And then there is the puppy who learned that every dog or person means a party. Running up to meet dog after dog, person after person can make seeing another dog extremely exciting, until the leash prevents the puppy from getting there. Hello, frustration. If that was your puppy, you were probably following common advice.
beats.show: A row of happy dog icons appears, then a leash tightens between the puppy and the next dog and a small red label appears: 'Frustration'.

beats.say: Socialization isn't about checking off a list of people, dogs, places, and experiences. It's about helping a puppy build positive, flexible associations while giving them appropriate support and choice. Socialization is one ingredient in the larger picture we need to consider when we're trying to understand behavior.
beats.show: The party row clears and the 'Socialization' chip drops into the bowl beside the earlier chips.

scenes.heading: Age
scenes.visual_concept: Bowl scene. Age chip, life-stage ruler with adolescence and social maturity bands, Teen and Adult party cards, the dog park card, then the senior dog with icons, everyday interactions and a lowering tolerance meter. The bowl's eight ingredient chips, in order: Genetics and temperament, Prenatal environment, Breed traits, Socialization, Age, Past experiences, Training tools and methods, Pain and discomfort (shared module video/scenes/c1_bowl.js).

beats.say: Ingredient five, age. Adolescence runs from about six to eighteen months, up to two years in some big breeds. Think teenager with fur: big feelings, less self-control.
beats.show: On the first sentence the 'Age' chip drops in and the bowl shifts left; on 'Adolescence runs', a life-stage ruler draws beneath it with a shaded band labeled 'Adolescence, 6 to 18 months'.

beats.say: Then comes social maturity, when your dog becomes an adult, between about one and three years. This is when reactivity or aggression often shows up or gets louder.
beats.show: A second band shades in, 'Social maturity, 1 to 3 years', and pulses as a small volume icon turns up above it.

beats.say: Many dogs also get pickier about other dogs as they grow up. It's like a teenager who wants to go to parties and make a ton of friends. As an adult, they'd rather skip the party and see a few close friends.
beats.show: Two small cards appear under the ruler: 'Teen' with a party-popper icon and a crowd of little dots, then 'Adult' with a coffee icon and three dots, under the label 'More selective with age'.

beats.say: That's normal, not a problem. But the dog who loved the dog park at one may not want it at three, and pushing them can end in a fight.
beats.show: A small dog park card appears with a trees icon: 'Age 1: loved it' with a green check, then 'Age 3: not anymore' with an amber caution badge.

beats.say: Senior dogs change too. Sore joints, fading senses, or changes in memory can affect how much they want to deal with the little things they used to tolerate. A dog who once ignored being bumped, crowded, startled, or bothered may have less patience for those interactions as they get older.
beats.show: The cards clear; an older dog appears with small icons for sore joints, fading vision, hearing and memory. Around the dog, everyday interactions appear one per word: Bumped, Crowded, Startled, Bothered. A 'Tolerance' meter gradually lowers.

scenes.heading: Past experiences
scenes.visual_concept: Bowl scene. Past experiences chip and a lightning strike on a one-event timeline; a person, dog and toy sequence that repeats with the dog's response growing; a repeating encounter strip where the response comes sooner each time; then the lawn path with a new path forming. The bowl's eight ingredient chips, in order: Genetics and temperament, Prenatal environment, Breed traits, Socialization, Age, Past experiences, Training tools and methods, Pain and discomfort (shared module video/scenes/c1_bowl.js).

beats.say: Ingredient six, past experiences. A single event can be enough: if an off-leash dog rushes yours once, they may never forget it.
beats.show: The 'Past experiences' chip drops in and a lightning bolt strikes a single point on a short timeline labeled 'One event'.

beats.say: Repeated experiences can shape behavior too. Imagine someone repeatedly takes an item away from your dog. Your dog may start reacting when that person approaches while they have something.
beats.show: A person icon approaches a dog icon with a toy and takes the toy away. The sequence repeats three times, and each time the dog's warning marks grow bigger as the person approaches.

beats.say: And the more a dog practices a response, the easier that response can become. Practice makes patterns stronger. A dog that repeatedly barks, lunges, freezes, or snaps in a particular situation may begin to do it sooner and more automatically the next time.
beats.show: Three rows show the same encounter repeated; in each row the red response marker lands earlier along the row, with labels '1st', '5th', '20th'.

beats.say: It's like a path across a lawn: walk it every day and it wears in, until it's the way you go without thinking. The good news is we can build a new path.
beats.show: The rows fade into a faint dotted line across a green lawn that thickens into a worn path, and on 'the good news' a fresh green dotted path sketches in beside it.

scenes.heading: Training tools and methods
scenes.visual_concept: Bowl scene. Training tools chip with red-outlined tool tags; a dog surrounded by daily-life icons each linked to 'Human decides'; a 'Boss?' crown appears and fades; 'Suppress' over a dog replaced by 'Understand' and 'Help'; then a green heart pulses over the bowl. The bowl's eight ingredient chips, in order: Genetics and temperament, Prenatal environment, Breed traits, Socialization, Age, Past experiences, Training tools and methods, Pain and discomfort (shared module video/scenes/c1_bowl.js).

beats.say: Ingredient seven, training tools and methods. The tools and techniques we use also affect behavior. Research links harsh methods with more fear, stress, and aggression. Think leash jerks, prong, choke or shock collars, and pinning a dog down.
beats.show: The 'Training tools and methods' chip drops in and a short row of red-outlined tags appears beside it, one per phrase: Leash pops, Prong and choke collars, Shock collars, Alpha rolls.

beats.say: And when a dog reacts to something in their environment, it is not because they're trying to be the boss. Think about how much of your dog's life you already control. You decide where they sleep, when they go outside, where they go, how long they stay there, when they eat, and when they get access to the things they need and enjoy.
beats.show: The tags clear; a dog icon sits at center and icons appear around it one per phrase: Bed, Door, Walk, Time, Food, Toys, Outside. Each connects to a small 'Human decides' label.
beats.onscreen: You already control most of their world

beats.say: A dog reacting to something in their environment isn't trying to take over the household or establish rank. They're responding to something happening in that moment, not trying to change their place in the family.
beats.show: The life icons fade; a crown labeled 'Boss?' appears over the dog and fades away. The dog stays, facing a small trigger icon in front of them.
beats.onscreen: A reaction isn't a power struggle

beats.say: The idea that dogs need to be dominated has led to tools and techniques designed to suppress behavior through force or intimidation. But suppressing behavior isn't the same as understanding why a dog is responding that way and helping them change that response. We will get into this much more later.
beats.show: 'Suppress' appears in red over the dog icon and fades away; the words 'Understand' and 'Help' replace it in green.

beats.say: If you've used any of these, be kind to yourself. You did your best, and now you know more. A trainer who works without force can help you switch safely to a comfortable harness.
beats.show: Everything fades as a green heart icon pulses once over the bowl.

scenes.heading: Pain and discomfort
scenes.visual_concept: Bowl scene. Pain chip drops in; a dog with small body indicators and six sensitivity icons; a dog standing normally with faint question marks, then a second panel of the same dog avoiding a reaching hand; a sudden-change arrow that branches to Behavior and Physical health. The bowl's eight ingredient chips, in order: Genetics and temperament, Prenatal environment, Breed traits, Socialization, Age, Past experiences, Training tools and methods, Pain and discomfort (shared module video/scenes/c1_bowl.js).

beats.say: Ingredient eight, pain and discomfort. A dog who is in pain can have a lower tolerance for their environment.
beats.show: The 'Pain and discomfort' chip drops into the bowl. A dog appears with small indicators at different areas of the body, then icons pop in one per word: Touch, Bumping, Approach, Handling, Noise, Movement.

beats.say: And pain isn't always obvious. Dogs don't always limp, cry, or show us exactly where something hurts. A change in behavior may sometimes be one of the first clues that something isn't right.
beats.show: The icons clear; the dog stands normally while faint question marks appear around them. A second panel shows the same dog leaning away from a hand reaching toward them.

beats.say: That's why a change in behavior, especially a sudden change, is worth taking seriously. A veterinarian can help determine whether pain, illness, or another underlying physical condition could be contributing to the behavior.
beats.show: The panels clear; a sudden-change arrow appears beside a dog and leads to a veterinarian icon, which branches to 'Physical health' and 'Behavior'.

beats.say: Even when a physical condition is contributing, addressing the behavior itself is still important.
beats.show: The 'Pain and discomfort' chip glows in the bowl while the veterinarian and Behavior icons are framed together with the label 'Both matter'.

scenes.heading: Putting it together
scenes.visual_concept: The bowl at center with all eight chips dropping in as they are named; then the visible behavior at the top with the ingredient chips beneath it, partly hidden below a surface line; then the view shifts toward the surrounding context as a transition to the next chapter, and a short Calling All Dogs logo close. Bowl chips, in order: Genetics and temperament, Prenatal environment, Breed history and purpose, Socialization, Age, Past experiences, Training tools and methods, Pain and discomfort (shared module video/scenes/c1_bowl.js).

beats.say: By now, you can see that a dog's behavior usually isn't explained by one thing. Genetics and temperament, prenatal environment, breed history and purpose, socialization, age, pain and discomfort, past experiences, and the methods used with the dog can all become ingredients in the behavior we see.
beats.show: The mixing bowl returns to center screen with eight blank chips above it. The chips drop in as they are named: Genetics and temperament, Prenatal environment, Breed history and purpose, Socialization, Age, Pain and discomfort, Past experiences, Training tools and methods.
beats.onscreen: Behavior is shaped by many factors

beats.say: But not all of those ingredients are visible on the surface. What we see is the behavior. And to understand it more fully, we need to look at what is happening around it.
beats.show: The bowl clears. The visible behavior (a dog barking) sits at the top above a surface line, while the eight ingredient chips appear beneath it, partly hidden and faded.

beats.say: That's where we'll go next.
beats.show: The view shifts from the visible behavior toward the surrounding context: simple situation elements appear around the dog and an arrow points forward to the next chapter. The Calling All Dogs logo closes the video.
